gylopsangilopsandancbylops.c: GYLOPS, Angilops and Ancbylops, is a Tu - mour or Swelling in the great Corner of the Eye by the. Root of the Nose, either with or. without an Inflammation. iEGYTIACUM, fc. Vnguemum, in Pharmacy, is a kind of Detersive Ointment, described by Mefue; and is so called from its black Colour, like the Hue of an Egyptian.

gatarrhus.c: GATARRHUS, is a Defluxion of Humours from the Head towards the Parts under it, as the Nostrils, Mouth, Lungs, & ' c. Some distinguish it by the Name of Loryzn, when it falls on the No - ftrils, by that of Bronchus when on the Jaws; and by the Word plume, N it it falls on the Breast.

gor.c: GOR, is by the Botanists used to signs the inward soft pithy and spongy part of any Tree or Plant which they call also Medulla and Matrix Arboris.

gornachinepowder.c: GORNACHINE Powder, the fame with what is sometimes called the Earl of Warwick ’. ? Powder, and by Foreign Writers frequently Pulvis de tri - bus; it is a purging Powder made of equal parts of Antimonium Diaphoreticum, Diagridium, and Cream of Tartar.

graft.c: GRAFT is a Sea Word figmfying all manner of Lines, Nets, Hooks, c. which serve for Fifli - ing; and because those that use the Fiftung Trad use final ! Vessels, such as Ketches, Hoys and Smacks, c, they call all such little Vessels Small Craft.

gabel.c: GABEL, according to some of our Ancient Records, Statutes, Charters, &c.. signifies a Rent, Custom, or Duty yielded or done to the King, or any other Lord, not by Contract: or Bargain, but imposed by the Will of the Lord. Both the Word and Thing it self is grown quite out of Fashion in England, where no Duty can be imposed upon the Subject but by Ad of Parliament; but in France it is still practiced, where it signifies an Ex - case upon Salt, and is a very heavy one.

gabionsaterminfortification.c: GABIONS, a Term in Fortification, signifying Baskets made of Osier - Twigs, equally wide at the Top and Bottom, about four Foot in Diameter, and from five to fix high; which being filled with Earth, are sometimes used as Merlons for the Bat - teries, and sometimes as a Parapet for the Lines of Approach, when it is requisite to carry on the At - tacks through a Stony or Rocky Ground, and to advance them with extraordinary Vigour. They serve also to make Lodgments in some Polls, and to secure other Places from the Shot of the Ene - mies, who nevertheless endeavour to fet the Gabi - ons on Fire with Pitch ’ d Faggots, to render them useless.

gage.c: GAGE, when one Ship is to Windward of ano - ther, she is laid to have the Weather - gage of her: The Seamen call also trying how much Water a Ship draws Gaging, or rather Gauging of her -, and it is thus done; They drive a Nail into a Pike near the End, and then put down this Pike by the Rud - der till the Nail ketch hold under it, for then as many Feet as the Pike is under Water, is the Ship s Gage, or the Depth of Water ( he draws.

gageincommonlaw.c: GAGE, in Common Law, signifies a Pawn or Surety: See more in Wage.

galaxyorvia.c: GALAXY, or Via LaElea: See Milky - Way. GALE, the Sea Word for the blowing of the Wind at Sea: When the Wind blows not so hard but that a Ship can carry her Top - fails a Trip, ( that is, boiled up to the highest ) then they fay it is a Loom - Gale j when it blows very strong, they fay it is a stiff, or strong, or at least, a fresh Gale; but when it blows so hard and violently that a Ship cannot bear any Sail, they fay it blows a Storm. When two Ships are near one another at Sea, and there being but little Wind blowing, one of them finds more of it than the other, they lay that the Ship Gales away from the other.

galea.c: GALEA, is a Pain in the whole Head, lo called from the Likeness of the Place, because it takes in, or encompasses the whole Head like an Helmet j in Latine Galea. Blanchard. TT, e.
GALEA is likewise used when the Head of the Foetus is clothed with Part of the Membrane called Amnion, as it comes into the World they lay then it hath a Galea, Blanchard.

galenic.c: GALENIC - MEDICINE, is that Pfiyfick which is built upon the Principles of Galen, and therefore they are Galenifts who embrace the Foundations of that Art, which are fetched from Galen and his Prin - ciples; though tis now frequency opposed to the Chymical Method of Practice, which, they fay, is much Shorter. Blanchard.

That the Gall or Bile, being to be mix ’ d with the Chyle, as it comes out of the Stomach into the Duodenum, could be no where so conveniently secerned from the Blood, as where the Liver is plac ’ d; had also all the Branches of the Celiack Arteries, carried all the Blood to the Liver, from which the Gall was to be separated: It is evident, considering the nearness of the Liver to the Heart, and tHe In - testing Motion of the Blood, That so viscid a Secretion, as the Gall is, could never have been separated by any Gland in that Place. In this Cale therefore, Nature is forced to alter her con - ffant Method of fending the Blood to all Parts of the Body by the Arteries; and here she forms a Vein, ( which is no Branch of the Cava, as all other Veins are ) and by it she fends the Blood from the Branches of the Mefenterickand Celiack Arteries, ( after having palled thro ’ all the In - testiness, Stomach, Spleen, Caule, and Pancreas ) to the Liver. By which extraordinary Contri - vance, the Blood is brought a great Way about, before it arrive at the Liver; and its Celerity is extremely diminish ’ d: So that all the Corpuscles which are to form the Gall, may have sufficient Time to Attract one another, and to Unite, be - fore they come to their secerning Vessel. And thus the Ule of the Vena Porta is loundout. And moreover he computes, that since a Branch of the Mefeuterick Artery is to its cor - relponding Branch of the Porta, as ? to,; there - fore the Blood in the Branches of the Porta moves above times flower than it does in the Trunk of the Melenterick Artery; and this only on the Account of the Encrease of the Diameters of the Vessels. Thus Nature provides for the forming of the Gall, in that Blood which passes thro ’ the Me - lenterick Artery. Next he enquires what Care is taken about that which is convey ’ d by the Ce - lick Artery to the Liver. For it Items it was ne - eelfary to fend a larger Quantity of Blood thither, than could be disposed of thro ’ the Intestines. Part of the Blood of the Celiack Artery is spread upon the Stomach and Caul, and its Velocity dtminilhed, as we have been in the Intestines: But Bill all the Blood which those Parts could receive, was not sufficient for the Liver; and there was no room for the Division and Expia - ting of the Vessels thro ’ finch a large Space as the Mesentery, and the long Tradl of the Guts. And therefore here Nature hath a new Contri - vance to abate the Velocity of the Blood, ( to which the Intestine Motion is always Proportion - nal ); which is, by emptying the Blood entire - ly out of the Vessels, into a large spongy Bow - el, the Spleen; which seems to be a Cistern pro - vided for that very Intent and Purpose. And the Circumference of the Celiack Artery being half an Inch, or. its Square is. And there - fore the Square of the Splenick, which is a Branch of it, cannot be above.. Now the Dimen - lions of the Spleen are Inches long, or m Breadth, and in Thickness. He makes therefore this ealy Suppofttion, That it is a Cylinder df Inches Diameter. Wherefore the Square of its Circumference being, the Blood must move above " Q Times flower in it, than in the Be - ginning of The Splenick Artery; and is longer before it gets to the Liver, than that which passes through all the Intestines. From all this Art and Contrivance, it is an evident Demonflration, That the Intent of Na - ture was to diminish the Velocity of the Blood and that such a flow Motion is absolutely ne - ceflary for the secerning of the Bile in the Liver. The Particles which compose the Gall, he ihews, bear a very line Proportion to the reft of the Blood; as is evident from that great Qpan - city of Blood which is carried to the Liver, and the small Quantity of Bile which is separated from it. In a large Dog, whose Dublus Chole - dottius was near as big as a Man ’ s, I could never gather above two Drachms in an Hour. Now there is thrown into the Aorta every Hour a - bout Ounces of Blood; and it appears by the Proportions of the Arteries, that the Mefen trick and Celiack are to the reft, as to. And therefore Ounces of Blood are carried every Hour to the Liver. And since only two Drams of Gall are separated from it, ' the Blood must be to the Blood, at least as is to. Tis by Reason of this small Proportion of the Bile to the Blood, that it was so necessary to allow so much Time for the Attraction of the Particles which form the Bile. From this Contrivance all of the Porta, the Bile receives another Advantage, not less confi - durable than the Diminution of the Velocity of the Blood: And that is, the Blood palling thro so many different Parts before it comes to the Liver, parts with the greatest Share of its Lympha. By which means, the Particles composing the Bile approaching nearer towards one another are by their mutual Attraction sooner united. And the Consideration of these two Contri - hances does highly ( he thinks ) confirm the Truth of his Theory of Animal Secretion. For the Di - minution of the Velocity of the Blood, and the Substraction of the Lympha, cap agree in no other End, than the uniting the Particles of Bile.

gallactophori.c: GALLACTOPHORI, are Du & us's which carry; Milk, and convey the Chyle ( as some Modern Au - thors have fancied ) a strait way from the Guts to the Glandules of the Breasts; yet the Arteries are more properly so called, because they carry the Chyle along with the Blood to the Breasts, wherein the Milk is separated and reserved for the Use of the Foetus.

gallery.c: GALLERY, in a Ship, is that Beautiful Frame which is made upon the Stern without - board, into which there is a Passage out of the Captain ’ s Cab - bin, which is called the Great Cabbin and these Galleries are indeed rather for Stately Shew, and the Captain ’ s Pleasure, than any other Benefit; for in Ships of War all open Galleries of this kind are to be avoided, in regard of the Facility of an Ene - my ’ s Entrance, and boarding of the Ship that way.

GALLERY of a Mine, is any Branch of it carried on towards any Place. For the Besiegers, and the Besieged, do carry each of them Galleries or Branches under Ground, insearch of one ano - thers Mines, which often meet and destroy one another,

galleryinfortification.c: GALLERY, in Fortification, is a covered Walk, ’ the Sides whereof are Musket - proof, consisting of a Double Row of Planks lined with Plates of Iron j the Top being sometimes covered with Earth or Turf, to hinder the Effed of the Artificial Fire of the Besieged. These Galleries are frequently made use of in the Moat already filled with Faggots and Bavins, to the end that the Miner may approach safe to the Face of the Bastion when the Artillery of the opposite Flank is dismounted.

galreda.c: GALREDA, a thick vifeous Juice that is ex - traded by boiling from the Gristly Parts of Ani - mals, and is usually called a Geliy.

gang.c: GANG: To Man the Boat, in the Sea Phrase, is to put a Gang of Men ( whichis a Company ) into her: They are commonly called the Coxfwain s Gang who hath the Charge of her.

gangway.c: GANGWAY, signifies all the several Entrances, Ways, orPaffages from one Part of the Ship to the other; and whatsoever is put in any one of these Passages, are said to relaid or putid the Gangway.

ganglion.c: GANGLION, is an Humour in the Tendinous and Nervous Parts, proceeding from a Fall, Stroke, orotherwife: It refills if stirred; if pressed upon the Side, is not diverted, nor can be turned round. B'anchard. ' c

gangrene.c: GANGRENE, is a Cadaverous Corruption ol a Part, attended with a beginning of Stink, Blackness, and Mortification. Blanchard. GARB

garbtheterminheraldry.c: GARB, the Term in Heraldry for a Wheat - Sheaf.

garbard.c: GARB ARD - PLANK, the first Plank of a Ship fastened on her Keel; as

garboard.c: GARBOARD - STRAKE, is the first Seam in a Ship next to the Keel.

garddu.c: GARD DU - CORD, or Gard - du - Gut: See Gar - decant.

gardecautorgard.c: GARDECAUT, or Gard - du - cord, is that which flops the Fusy of a Watch when wound up, and for that end is driven up by the String j some call it Guard - Cock,, others Gard - du - Gut.

gardeynedelesglise.c: GARDEYNE DEL ESGLISE, or Church - War - dens, are Officers chosen in every Parifli to have the Care and Cuftodyof the Church Goods; and they may have an A Elion for the Goods of the Clstrch, and divers other things they may do for the Benefit of the Church: They are to join with the Overfeers for the making of Rates, and other Provision for, the Poor of the Parifli.

gardianorguardian.c: GARDIAN, or Guardian, signifies generally him that hath the Custody or Charge of any Person or thing; but most commonly him that hath the Ed - cation or Protection of such People as are not of sufficient Discretion to guide themselves and their Affairs, being indeed as largely extended as their Tutor and Curator among the Civilians; for whereas Tutor is he that hath the Government of a Youth until he come to fourteen Years of Age; and Cura - tor, he that hath the imposition and ordering his fi - late afterwards, Until he attain to the Age of five and twenty Years; or that hath the Charge of a Frantick Person during his Lunacy; both these with us are called Guardians. A Tutor is either Tefl ament arius, or a Part ore da - tus ex Lege Atilia; or lastly, Legitimus: So we have three forts of Guardians in England, one or - gained by the Father in his last Will, another ap - pointed by the Judge, the third cast u'poti the Mi - nor by the Law and Custom of the Land. As to the first: of these, a Man having Goods or Chattels, may appoint a Guardian to the Body or Person of his Child, by his Last Will and Tefta - intent, until he come to the Age of fourteen Years, and so the disposing and ordering of his Estate lo long as he thinks meet, which is commonly to one and twenty Years of Age. The fame he may do of Lands not holden in Capite, or by Knight ’ s - Ser - vice; but the ancient Law in this Case is very much altered, and in all Cafes gives the Father Po - wer to appoint a Guardian for his Child; but if the Father order no Guardian to his Child, the Ordinary may appoint one to manage his Goods and Chat - tels till the Age of fourteen Years; at which time he may choose him another Guardian, as by the Civil Law he may his Curator, for this Rule holds, that is, ’ Invito Curator non dat'ur. And for his Lands the next a - kin on that Side, by which the Land cometh not, still be Guardian, ' who was formerly called Guardian in Soccage,,

GARDIAN, or Guardian of the Spiritualties, is he to whom the Spiritual ’ furifdiEiionof any Dio - case is committed during the Vacancy of the See. And the Guardians of the Spiritualities may either be Guardiatt in Law, or Jure Magififatus, as the Archbishop of any Diocese within his Province; or Guardians by Delegation, as he to whom the Archbishop or Vicar - General doth for the time de - put. t

gardian.c: GARDIAN, or rather Warden of the Cinque - Ports, is a principal Magistrate that hath the JurifdiEtion of those Havens in the South East - part of England, which are commonly called; The CinquS Ports; that ish the five Ports or Havens; who there hath all that Jurifditfbon that the Lord High Admiral of England hath in Places not exempt.

gargareon.c: GARGAREON, the fame with the Epiglottis or Cover, of the Wind - pipe; which fee.

gargarism.c: GARGARISM, is a Liquid Medicine which is used to cleanse the Mouth and the adjacent Parts, by gurgling or moving it up and down in the Throat without swallowing; and it is either a Be coElion, wherein convenient Syrups are dissolved, or distilled Waters mixed with Syrups, and some - times with Mineral Spirits. Blanchard.

garland.c: GARLAND, in a Ship, is that Collar of Rope which is wound about the Head of the Main - mall, to keep the Shrouds from galling.

garnet.c: GARNET, is a Tackle in a Ship, having a Pen - dant coming from the Head of the Main - mail, with a Block strongly seized to the Main - stay just over tfie Hatch - way; in which Block is reeved the Run - ner, which hath a Hook at one End, in which is hitched the Slings; and at the other End is a Double Block, in which the Fall of the Runner is reeved, that so by it any Goods or Casks that are not over - heavy, may be haled andhoifed into, or out of the Ship; when this Garnet is not used, it ’ s fastened a " long by the Stay at the Bottom of it,

garnishee.c: GARNISHEE, is taken for the Party in whose Hands Money is attached within the Liberties of the City of London, so used in the Sheriff of Lon - don s Court, because he has had Garnijhment or Warning, not to pay the Money, but to appear and answer to the Plaintiff ’ s Creditors Suit.

garnishmentinlaw.c: GARNISHMENT, in Law, is a Warning gi - ven to one for his Appearance, for the better furniffi - ing of the Cause and Court; as if one is sued for the Detinue of certain Evidences and Charters, and faith, Thatothe Evidences were delivered to him, not only by the Plaintiff, but another also; therefore prayeth that that other may be warned to plead with the Plaintiff, Whether the said Con - ditions be performed or no ? And in this Petition he is said to pray Garnijhment: Neve Book of Entries Sol. xi. Col..

garrison.c: GARRISON, is a certain Number of Officers and Soldiers that defend a Place.

garteraterminheraldry.c: GARTER, a Term in Heraldry, signifying the Moiety or half a Bend: See Bend.

gasaword.c: GAS, a Word used by Van Helmont, and seems designed to signify in General a Spirit not capable of being coagulated: But he uses it loosely in ma - ny Senses; as he calls the Vital Principle in Man, Gas Vitale; that Siilpherous or Arsenical, or any other way noxious Damp which is found in some Mines, he calls Gas Bmgue Sulphureum Nay, some - times he calls the Air its Gas Ventofum, as he doth Water Gas Salium - y and in short, speaks very union - telligibly and inconsistently about it, as the Chymist ’ s Manner is in other things.

gasterocnemium.c: GASTEROCNEMIUM, is the Calf of the Leg, whence its Muscles are called G fierocncmii, from their swelling like a Belly: Therefore two of these Muscles are called Gafterocnefnii.

gasterocnemiusexternus.c: GASTEROCNEMIUS Externus, also Gemellus is a Muscle of the Tarsus, so called, because ( ' with the Soleus or tnternus of that Name ) it composed the Calf of the Leg: It is also called Gemellus, from its being as it were double. It has two diilinEt Fleshy Originations, from the fuperiorand hindmost Parts of each Tubercle of the lower Appendage of the Thigh Bone, which in their Descent are each dilated into two large Fleshy Bellies, the innermoA of Which is thickest and largess, having each a dis - fering Series of Fleshy Fibres, and join to each o ther near where they make a broad strong Ten - don, ’ G A U don, which narrowing it self, joins with the great Tendon of the Gajlerocnemius Interims, four Fingers breadth above itslnfertion to the Os Calebs. When this Muscle adls, the Foot is said to be extended or pulled backwards, which Motion of it is very ne - pessary in Walking, Running, Leaping, and Stan - ding on Tiptoe, &c. Hence it is, those that walk touch, that carry heavy Burthens, Chairs, &c. and who wear low - heel ’ d Shooes, have these Mu - scales larger than others. GASTEROCNEMiUS Interims, is a Muscle of the Foot, which is placed under the Gajlerocnemius Externus and Plantar is. It is also called Soleus from its Figure, resembling a Sole - Fish. It ’ s externally fleshy Partis covered with a Transparent Tendi - nous Expansion, which makes it appear of a livid Colour. Its Beginning is partly Tendinous, but chiefly Fleshy from the hindermost Part of the up - per Appendix of the Fibula, and Back - part of the Tibia, that is below the Insertion of the Subpoplite - us, and increasing to a large Fleshy Belly composed of various Orders of Fleshy Fibres, some of them underneath aptly expressing the Figure of the Top of a Feather, whose Stamina here being Tendinous, join with the great Tendon, which is about a Fin - ger ’ s Breadth in Length, and inserted to the Superior and hindmost Part of the Os Calebs. The Foot, to - gether with the Toes, being as it were a Leaver to the whole Body, ought therefore to be attended with Muscles of great Strength to extend it; where - fore we find these Muscles so much to exceed the Antagonist, the Tis a us Anticus, as well in the advan - tageous Conftru & ion of their differing Series of Fleshy Fibres, as their Magnitude and Insertion at the Extremity of the Os Calebs, whereby they are not only rendred Serviceable in Walking, Running, Leaping, &c. but do also support the Tibia in Stan - ding, left the superincumbent Preffureofthe Weight of the Body should make them incline forwards at their Articulations with the Talus.

gastraoepiploica.c: GASTRAOEPIPLOICA, is the Vein and Artery which goes to the Ventricle and Cawl.

gastrorhaphia.c: GASTRORHAPHIA, is a Connexion or a Su - ture in the Wounds of the Abdomen. GASTROTOMYj the cutting of the Abdomen: See Ccefarean SeQion.

gate.c: GATE of the Sea, or a Sea - Gate, is when two Ships lie aboard one another in a Wave or Billow, and by that Means Sometimes become Rib - broken.

gavelinlaw.c: GAVEL, in Law, signifies Tribute, Toll, Cu - stom. Yearly Rent, Payment, or Revenue, of which there are leveral Kinds, as Gavel - Corn, Ga - vel - Malt, Out - Gavel, Gavel - Fodder, &c.

gavelet.c: GAVELET, is a special and ancient kind of Ges favit used in Kent, where the Custom of Gavel - kind continncth, whereby the Tenant shall forfeit his Lands and Tenements to the Lord of whom he holdeth, if he withdraw from him his due Rents and Services. Mr. S. in his History of Gavel - bind, says, That this Gavelet was not a Rent or Service, but signified a Rent or Service withheld, denied, or detained, causing the Forfeiture of the Tenement to the Lord; with which the Lord Coke agrees, where be says, That Gaueletum is as much as to fay, to cease, or to let to pay the Rent. And it seems this Writ lay in London as well as Kent.

gavel.c: GAVEL - KIND, signifies, in Law, a Custom, whereby the Land of the Father is equally divided at his Death among all his Sons, or the Land of the Brother at his Death equally divided among all his Brethren, if he have no Issue of his own. This Cu - stom is still in force in divers Places of England e - specially in Ken ’ Urchenfield in Hertford / hire, and elsewhere, though with some Difference: And all Gavel - kind Land in Wales are made descendible ro the Heirs, according to the Course of the Com - mon Law. In Gavel - kind, tho ’ the Father be hang - ed, the Son shall inherit; for their Custom is. The Father to the Bough, the Son to the Plough,
GAVEL - MADE, was the Duty of mowing Grass, or cutting Meadow Land, required by the Lord from his Cuilomary Tenant: So,
GAVEL - REP, or Bedreap, was the Duty of Reaping at the Bid at Command of the Lord. G A BELLI N G - Men. Tenants which paid a Reserved Rent, besides feme Customary Duties to be done by them.

gemellus.c: GEMELLUS, is a Muscle of the Cubit, so cal - led from its double Origine; it ariseth first Tendi - nous from the superior Part of the inferior Costa of the Scapula internally, and as it passeth between the two round Muscles, it grows Fleshy, and in its Descent joineth with its other Beginning, which a ? rises broad and Fleshy from the upper and back - part of the Os Humeri, under the Deltoid Muscle; and being Tendinous on the outside, and Fleshy within, is so inferred to the fiiperibr and external Part of the XJlna, called Olecr anoth and Ancon, or the Elbow. Its Use is to extend the Cubit If we examine the two Beginnings of this Muscle, we Shall find them interwoven with various Orders of Fibres, whereby it is rendred capable of perform - ing the Extenfioh of the Cubit with a greater Strength; Which appears in Tumblers when they afe walking on their Hands, who by an immediate Extension of their Cubits, can return to their Feet.

generation.c: GENERATION, is the Production of anything in a Natural Way, which before was not in Being: For when in any Parcel of Matter there is produced such a Concurrence of all those Accidents which ( ’ tis agreed ) are necelTary and sufficient to constitute a determinate Species of things Corporeal; we then fay a Body belonging to that Species is generated. So that here, properly speaking, no New Substance, but only a new Ejfcntial Denomination, Modificati - on, or Manner of Existence is produced or genera - ted: And when that Union of Accidents which denominates a Body generated is destroyed and dis - solved, that Body losing its ElTential Modification is said to be Corrupted.

GENERATION. As to what the Moderns, - in their Discoveries by Microlcopes, have ad - anc ’ d on this Subject, you will and by com - paring the Observations and Discoveries of Dr. Harvey, S. Malpighii ) Dr. de Graaf and M. Leewenhoeck, with one another: And these Three Things seem to me very probable. That And may G E N mals are ex Anifnalculo.. That tlie Animalcules are originally in Semine Marium, & non in Same - ne.. That they can never come Forward, nor fee Formed into Animals of the respective Kind, without the Ova in Faminis. The Firfl of these Teems probable from these Observations;. That l'ome such Thing has been so often observ ’ d by Malpighius in the Cica - trical a of an Egg before Incubation, as the Rudi - ments of an Animal in the Shape of a Tadpole; as may be seen in his First, and in his Repeated Observations de Formatione Full in Ovo.. The sudden Appearance and Displaying of all the Parts, after Incubation, makes it probable, that they are not then actually Formed out of a Fluid, but that the Stamina of them have been formerly there Existent, and are now expanded. The First Part of the Chick which is discovered with the Naked Eye is, you know, the Fundi um S aliens, and that not till Three Days and Nights of Inch - bastion be pall: And then on the Fifth Day the Rudiments of the Head and Body do appear. This made Dr. Harvey conclude, that the Blood had a Being before any other Part of the Body, and that from it all the Organs of the Fat us were both Formed and Nourished but by Maipighius ’ s Observations, we find that the Parts are then only so far Extended, as to be made visible to the Naked Eye, and that they were actually Exi - gent before, and discernible by GlaJJes. After an Incubation of Hours, are to be seen the Head, the Eyes, and the Carina, with the Vertebra, distinct, and the Heart. After Hours its Pulse is visible, and all the other Parts more distinct, which cannot be discens by the Naked Eye before the Beginning of the Fifth Day from whence it seems very probable that even the so early Discovery of thole Parts of die Foetus by the Microscope, is not the Discerning of Parts newly Formed, but only more Dilated and Ex - tended by receiving of Nutriment from the Colli - quamentum; so that they seem all to have been actually Existent before the Incubation of the Hen. And what Swammardam has discover ’ d in the Tranjmutation of Insects, gives no final Light to this, whilst he makes appear in the Explanation of the th Table of the General History of Infedts, that in thole large Erne as which feed upon Cab - base, if they be taken about the Time they retire to be Transform'd into Aurelias, and plunged of - ten in warm Water to make a Rupture of the Outer Skin, you will discern, through the Tranfpa - rence of their Second Membrane, all the Parts of the Butterfly, the Trunk, Wings, Feelers, &c. folded up: But, that after the Eruca is Changed into an Aurelia, - n n. oTthele Parts can be discens, they are so drench with Moil tire, though they be there actually Formed. Another Consideration is from the Analogy, which we may suppose between Plants and Ani - mals. All Vegetables, we fee, do proceed ex Plan - tula, the Seeds of V getables being nothing else but Little Plants of the fame Kind folded up in Coats and Membranes; and from hence we may probably Conjecture, that so curiously an Orga - sized Creature, as an Animal, is not the sudden ProduCt of a Fluid, or Colliquamentum, but does much rather proceed from. an Animalcle of the fame Kind, and has all its little Members folded up according to their several Joints and Plicatures, which are afterwards Enlarged and Defended, as ; we see in Plants. Now though this Confidera -: tion alone may seem not to bear much Weight, !; yet being joyned to. the two former, they do ] mutually strengthen each other. And indeed a I the Laws of Motion which are as yet difeovefd can give but a very Lame Account of the For mini of a Plant or Animal. We fee how wretchedly Des Cartes came off, when he began to apply them to this Subjedf. They are Formed by Laws yet Unknown to Mankind and it seems moll pro - table, that the Stamina of ail the Plants and Ani - mals that have been, or ever shall be in the World have been Formed ab Origine Mundi, by the Al - mighty Creator within the Firfl of each reigjedtive Kind. And he whoconfiders the Nature of Vi - flon, that it does not give us the True Magnitude, but the Proportion of Things, and that what seems to our Naked Eye but a Point, may truly be made up of as many Parts as seem to us to be in the Whole Visible World, will not think this an Absurd. or Impollible Thing. But the Second Thing which later Discoveries ha ve made probable is, " that these Animalcules are original ly in Semins Marium, & non in Fceminis: And this I Collect from thele Considerations . That there are Innumerable Anmalcula in Semine Mafculino Omnium Animalium. M. Lee - wenhoeck has made this so Evident by so many Observations, that I do not in the leal question the Truth of the Thing. . The Observing of the Rudiments of the Fcc - tm in Eggs, which have been Fecundated by the Male, and the seeing no such Thing in those which are not Fcecundated, as appears from Mal - pighius his Observations, makes it very ' probable, that these Rudiments proceeded originally from the Male, and not from the Female. . The Resemblance between the Rudiments of the Foetus in Ovo, both Before and After Inch - bastion, and the Animalcule, makes it very proba - ble, that they are One and the Same. The lame Shape and Figure which M. Leewenhoeck gives us of the Animalcule, Malpighius likewise gives us of the Rudiments of the Foetus, both before and after Incubation yea, and even the Foetus ’ s of Animals do appear so at firfl to the Naked Eye so that Dr, Harvey does acknowledge, that all Animals, even the moss Perfedl. are Begotten of a Worm. . This gives a Rational Account of Many Fetus ’ s at One Birth, especially that of the Coun less of Holland; and how, at leal, a Whole Clufler of Eggs in a Hen are Fecundated by One Coition of the Male. . This gives a New Light, as it were, to the Firfl Prophecy concerning the Mejflah, that the Seed of the Woman fball bruise the Head of the Ser - pent: All the reft of Mankind being thus moll Properly and Truly the Seed of the Man. . The Analogy I have already mention ’ d, which we may rationally suppose between the Manner of the Propagation of Plants and Animals, does likewise make this Probable. Every Herb and Tree bears its Seed after its Kind j which Seed is nothing else but a Little Plant of the fame Kind, which being thrown into the Earth, as in - to its Uterus, spreads forth its Roots, and receives its Nourishment, but has its Form within Jtfelfi and we may rationally conjecture some such Ana - logy in the Propagation of Animals. ' The / The Third Particular, which later Discoveries make probable, is, That Animals cannot be Formed bf tliele Animalcula without the Ova in Faminis, which are necessary for Supplying them with Proper Nutriment and this, these Confederations seem to evince, i. It is probable that an Animal - rule cannot come forward if it do not fall into a proper Nidus. This we see in the Cicatpicula in Eggs, and tho a Million of them should fall in - to One Egg, None of them would come forward, but what were in the Center of the Cicatricula and perhaps the Nidus, necessary for their Formation, is so proportioned. to their Bulk, that it can hardly contain more than One Animalcle; and this may. be the Reason why there are so Few Munflers. This we fee is absolutely necessary in Oviparis; and the only Difference which Seems. to be between them and the Fivipara in this Matter, is in this, That in the Latter the Ova are properly nothing more but the Cicatricula, with its Colliqua - mentum, so that the Foetus must spread forth its Roots into the Uterus to receive its Nourishment; but the Eggs in Oviparis ray be properly termed an Uterus in relation to the Foetus; for they con - tain, not only the Cicatricula with Its Amnion and Colliquamentum, which is the Immediate Nourift - ment of the Fat us, but also the Materials which are to be converted into that Colliquamentum so that the Foetus spreads forth its Roots no far - ther than into the White and Folk of the Egg, from whence it derives all its Nourishment. Now that an Animalcle cannot come forward without some such proper Nidus, M. Leewenhoeck will not rea - dily Deny; for if there were nothing Needful but their being thrown into the Uterus, I do not fee why many Hundreds of them should not come forward at Once, at least whilst scatter ’ d in lo large a Field. Now,. That this Cicatricula is not Originally In Utero, Seems Evident from the frequent Con - ceptions which have been found extra Uterum: Such as the Child which continued Tears in the Woman of Tholoufes Belly and the Little Foetus found in the Abdomen of Mad. de S. Mere, together with the TeJHcle Torn, and full of Clot - ted Blood such also seem to be the Foetus in the Abdomen of the Woman of Copenhagen, mentioned in the Nouvelles des Letters, for Sept.. all the Members of which were easily to be felt thro the Skin of the Belly, and which the had carried in her Belly for Tears: And. the Tears Gravida - tion related by Dr. Cole. Now granting once the Necessity of a Proper Nidus, for the Formation of an Animalcle into the Animal of its refpediive Kind, theie Observations make it probable, that the Testes are the Ovaria appropriated for this Use; for though the Animalcles coming thither in such Cafes, may seem to be Extraordi - nary, and that usually the Impregnation is in Ute - ro, yet it may be Collected from hence, that the Cicatricula or Ova to be Impregnated, are ’ in Tefii - bus Seem ine. s; for if it were not so, the Acc - dental coming of Animalcles Thither, could not make them come forward more than in any other Part of the Body, since they cannot be Formed and Nourijbed without a Proper Nidus. But,. It is acknowledge ’ d by all, that the Foetus in Utero, for some confierablc Time after Conception, has no Connexion with the Womb that it fits wholly loose to it, and is perfeeiiy a Little Round Egg with the Foetus in the Midst, which lends forth its Umbilical F efjcls by Degrees, and Voh L at ali lays hold on the Uterus. Now from hence it Seems evident, that the Cicatricula, which is the Fountain of the Animalcle s Nourishment, does not sprout from the Uterus, but has its Origine elsewhere, and falls in thither as into a fit Soil, from whence it may draw Nutriment for the Growth of the Foetus else it cannot be easily imagined how it should not have an Immediate Connexion with the Uterus from the Time of Conception. If you joyn all these Three Considerations to - gether, viz,, that an Animalcle esnnot Come for - ward without a Proper Nidus, or Cicatricula that there have been frequent Fcetuis extra Ute - rum; and that they have no Adhejjon to the Ute - rus for a considerable Time after Conception they seem to make it evident, that Animals cannot be Formed ex Animalculis without the Ova in Semi - nis. To all these I Shall subjoin the Proposal of an Experimentum Crucis, which may seem to determine whether the Tefles Famine a be truly the Ovaria; viz,. Open the Abdomen of the Females of some Kinds, aryl cut out these Ft sticks, and this will determine whether they be absolutely Necessary for the Formation of Animals. It is indeed difficult to conceive, how these Eggs Should be Impregnated per Semen Maris, both became there is no Connexion between the Tube and the Ovary for its Tranfiniffion; and for that Dr. Harvey could never discover any thing of it in Utero. But as to the la St, M. Leewenhoeck has cleared that Difficulty, by the Discovery of Innumerable Animalcula Seminis Maris in Corm - tus Uteri, and thole living a considerable time after Coition. And as to the Former, we may ei - ther suppose that there is stich an Inflation of the Tube, or. Cornua Uteri, tempore Coitionis, as makes them Embrace tire Ovaria, and stich an Approach of the Uterus and its Cornua, as that it may east - ly trahfinit the Seed into the Ovary: Or die, that the Ova are Impregnated by the Animalcles after they descend into the Uterus, and not in the Ovary The former seems probable for this Reason, that at lead a whole Clufler of Eggs in a Hen will hzFac un - dated by One Tread of the Cock now this Fecun - dation seems to be in the Fitellary, and not in the Uterus, as the Eggs pass along from Day to Day i For it can hardly be supposed that the Animalcles should liibfifi lo long, being scatter ’ d loosely in the Uterus, as to wait there, for many Days, for the Fecundation of the Eggs as they pals along. These a & ing, pull the Os Hyoides, &c, both upwards and forwards, and assist the Genioglojfa in thrusting the Tongue out of the Mouth.

genusinlogick.c: GENUS, in Logick, is an Idea so common and universal, that it extends it self also to other Vni - versal Ideas. Thus a Right - lined Figure of four Sides, is a Genus, in respect of a Parallelogram or a Trapezium. And in like manner Substance is the fame in refpetft of Substance extended, which is a Body; and Thinking Substance, which is a Spirit. The Logicians divides Genus into Summum or the highest Genus, which hath nothing above it to be a Species of: And Subalternate, which is sometimes, or in some respects, a Genus, and in others a Spe - cies.

geometry.c: GEOMETRY, originally signifies the Art of mea - suring the Earth, or any Distances or Dimensions: on or within it but ’ tis now used for the Science of Quantity, Ektenfion, or Magnitude, abjlracicdly confi - de red, without any regard to Matter. Geometry, very probably, had its first Rife in Egypt, where the Nile annually overflowing the Country, and covering it With Mud, obliged Men to distil - gush their Lands one from another, by the Consi - duration of their Figure; and to be able also to meaflite the Quantity of it, and to know how to plot it and lay it out again in its just Dimensions, Fi - gure, and Proportion: After which ’ tis likely a far - ther Contemplation of those Draughts and Figures, help ’ d them to difeovermany excellent and wonder - ful Properties belonging to them, which Speculati - dn Continually was improving, and is still to this ve - ry Day.

GEOMETRY is usually divided into Speculative and PraBical: The Former of which contemplates and treats of the Properties of continued Quantity abstractedly: And the Latter applies these Specula - tions and Theorems to Use and Practice, and to the Benefit and Advantage of Mankind. See You. II.

ginglimus.c: GINGLIMUS, is an Articulation of a Bone when it both receives and is received: Of this Art - cubation there are three forts. The First is when the End of a Bone has two Protuberances and one Cavity, and the End of the i Bone which is articulated with it has two Cavities and one Protuberance, as the Humerus and the Vena; or when a Bone at one Extremity receives another; Bone, and at its other Extremity it is received by the fame Bone, as the Padius and Vena. The Second Sort is when a Bone at One End re - chives another Bone, and at the other End is recti - ' vedby a third Bone, as the Vertebra do. The Third is when a Bone has a Cavity which i receives the long Process of another Bone which i Process turris'in the Cavity like the Axle - tree in a Wheel, as the second Vertebra of the Neck is art - culated with the first; but this is no true Gingli - mus.

given.c: GIVEN, is a Word often used in Mathematicks, and signifies something which is supposed to be known: Thus, if a Magnitude be known, or tha we can find another equal ta it, they fay, ’ Tis & given Magnitude, or that such a thing is given in Magnitude. If the Position of any thing be suppo - fed as known they fay. Given in Positions: Thus, if a Circle be a & ually defer ibed upon any Plane, they fay, its Center is given in Position; its Circum - ference is given in Magnitude j and the Circle both in Position and Magnitude. But a Circle may be given in Magnitude only; as when only its Diame - ter is given, but the Circle not actually deferibeef If the Kind or Species of any Figure be given, they fay, Given in Specie. If the Ratio between any two Quantities is known, they are laid to be given in Proportion. glandula.c: GLANDULA: A Glandule is a Substance of a peculiar Nature, Fleshy, White, or Gray; and it is two - fold: Adventitious, as those Kernels which are sometimes under the Arm - holes, and in the Neck, as the Kjng's - Evil; a Swelling in the La - lynx and middle of the Wind - pipe, &c. Or Perpetual and Natural, aS the Thymus, Pancreas, Glandula, Pinealis, &c. The Perpetual is again two - fold, ei - ther Conglobated in one entire Piece, which fends the separated Humour into the Veins, as the Pitui - tary Glandule, the Pinealis, the Glandules of the Mesentery of the Groins, &c. Or Conglomerated in a Clutter, which convey the Juice by their own Channels into some notable Cavities of the Body as the Pancreas, the Glandules of the Breajl, the Sa - live l Glandules, There are also discovered by Dr. Havers a fore of Glands, which he calls Mucilaginous Glands; which lee under Mucilaginous.

glandulapituitaria.c: GLANDULA Pituitaria, is little Body in the Sella Equina, a Place in the Brain lo called, cover ’ d oyer with the Pete Mirabile in many Brutes, but notion Men: It receives the Serous Humour from the Infindibulum and the Pete Mirabile, which it fends into the Jugular Veins and the Lymphatick Vessels. GLANDULiE Lumbares, are three Glands de - scribed by Bartholin, and by him so named, by rea - fon of their lying tiptin their Loins: He thus describes them, Pag.. of his Anot. Edit.. The two largest lie one upon another betwixt the descending Cava and Aorta, in that Angle which the Emulgents make with the Cava: The third being smaller stands over these under the Happen - dices of the Diaphragm. They have Communica - tion, or are knit to one another by small Lacfteal Branches, especially the two larger. He once thought them to supply the Place of the common Reeepticle in Man; that not being so plain in him as in several Brutes: But since a Recep - table is acknowledge ’ d as well in Men as Brutes, Dr. Whartons Opinion concerning their Ufefeems more probable, T c That That they supply the Place of thole larger Glands that are found in the Mefenteries of Brutes, but are not Natural to Men: And for this Reason he pre - fumes, That all such Animals as want those greater Glands in the Mesentery, have these Lumbares as well as Men. GLANDULiE Odorifer ce, are certain small Glan - rules discovered by that Accurate Anatomist Dr. Tyfon, in that Part of the Penis where the Prceputi - um is contiguous to the Bulanin; and he gives them this Name from the great Scent which their lepara. ted Liquor emits: In such Persons as have the Pre - puce longer than ordinary, these Glands are not only more, but larger, and separate a greater Quantity of their Juice, which lodging there, often grows acid, and corrodes the Glands: These are very conspicuous in most Quadrupeds, especially in Dogs and Boars.

glandulepennies.c: GLANDULE Pennies, feu Capsul a; Attrabilares, are Glands which lie between the Aorta and the Kidneys, a little above the Emulgent Vessels: They are two in Number, one on each Side, wrap ’ d up in Fat: They sometimes change their Situation, and their Figure is also various; for in some they are Jlound, in others Oval, Square, Triangular, of a Trapezial or Irregular Figure; the Right is ordinal - rily bigger than the Left, and each about the Bigness of a Nux Vomica. Their Use is not certainly known; they seem to separate a Liquor from the Arterial Blood before it goes to the Kidneys, for the liquefy - ing the Blood which is thick after it comes from them.

globeorsphere.c: GLOBE or Sphere, is a found solid Body, every Part of whose Surface is equally distant from a Point Within it; called its Center: and it may be conceived to be formed by the Revolution of a Semicircle round its Diameter. When such a Body as this hath all the Parts of the Earth and Sea drawn or delineated on its Sur - face, like as in a Map, and placed in their Natural Order and Situation, it is called the Terrestrial Globe. But if on its Surface it hath the fixed Stars and the Images of the Constellations drawn, together With the Circles of the Sphere below described, ’ tis then called the Celestial Globe. And when the following Circles are supposed to be described on the Convex Surface of a Sphere, which is hollow Within, and after this you imagine all Parts of the Sphere ’ s Surface to be cut away, except those Parts on which: such Circles are de - scribed, then that Sphere is called an Armillary Sphere, because it appears in the Form of fevers. ] Circular Rings or Bracelets put together in a due Position. There are. Ten Eminent Circles upon the Globe or of the Sphere; Six of which are called Greater, and the Four other Lesser Circles., A Great Circle of jhe Sphere is that whose Plane, passeth through the Center of the Sphere, and di - vides it into two equal Parts or Hemispheres. A Lesser Circle is that which is parallel to a Great -, ter, as the Tropickj and the Polar Circles are to the Equator, and as the Circles of Altitude are to the Horizon. Or Lesser Circles are such as do not divide the Globe into two equal Parts. The Greater Circles are, I. The Horizon, which is a broad wooden Cir - cle encompassing the Globe round about, having two Notches, the one in the North, the other in the South Part of it, for the Brazen Meridian to stand in. There are usually accounted two Horizons: First, The Visible or Sensible, which you may conceive to be made by some great Plain, or the Surface of the Sea; and which divides the Heavens into two Hemispheres, the one above, the other ( ap - parently ) below the Level of the Earth. This Circle determines the Riling and Setting of the Sun, Moon, or Stars, in any particular Latitude; for when any one of them comes just to the F. astern Edge of the Horizon, then we fay it Rifeth; and when it doth so at the Western Edge, we fay it Setteth. And from hence also the Altitude of the; Sun and Stars is accounted, which is their Height j in Degrees above the Horizon. II. The other Horizon is called the Peal or pat to - nal, and is a Circle which encompasses the Earth exatftly in the Middle, and whose Poles are the Zenith and Nadir; that is, two Points in its Axis, each Degrees distant from its Plain ( as the Poles of all Circles are ) and the one exatflly over our Heads, and the other directly under our Feet. This is the Circle which the Wooden Horizon on the Globe represents. On which Broad Horizon several Circles are drawn, the innermost of which is the Number of Degrees of the Twelve Signs of the Z zodiack., vi ? to each Sign: For the Ancient Astronomers ob - served the Sun in his ( apparent ) Annual Motion, to describe always one and the fame Line in Heaven, and never to deviate from this Track or Path to the North or South, as all the other Planets did more or less; and because they found the Sun also to Ihift, as it were backward, through all the parts of this Circle or Path, so that in his whole Years Course he; would Pjfe, Culminate, and Set with e - very Point of it; they distinguished the fixed Stars that appeared in or near this Circle into ' Twelve Confutations or Divisions, which they called Signs; and because they were most of them usually drawn in the Form of Animals, they called this Circle by the Name of the Zpdiack., and the very middle Line of it the Ecliptic.: And since every Circle was divided into Parts or Degrees, a twelfth twelfth part of that Number must be, the De - grees in each Sign, Next to this you have the Names of those Signs; next to this the Days of the Month, according to the Julian Account, or Old Stile, with the Calendar; and then another Calendar according to the Foreign Ac - count, called the New Stile. And without these is a Circle divided into Thirty two equal Parts, which make the Thirty two Rhumbs or Points of the Mariner ’ s Compass, with the first Letters of the Names annexed; andfince a thirty second Part of Degrees is Degrees Minutes, they account that each single Point of the Compalsis Degrees Minutes. The Vfes of this Circle in the Globe are, s. To determine the Riling and Setting of the Sun, Moon, or Stars, and to ftiew the Time of it by the help of the Hour - Circle and Index - as shall be Ihewed hereafter. . To limit the Increafeand Decreafeof the Day and Night: For when the Sun rises due East, and sets Weft, the Days are equal. But when he Rifeth and Setteth to the North of the East and Weft, the Days are longer than the Nights; as on the contrary, the Nights are longer than the Day, when the Sun Rifeth and Setteth to the Southward of the East and Weft Points of the Horizon. / ,. To ftiew the Amplitude of the Sun, or of any Star; and also, on what Point of the Compass it Ri - set and Setteth. ,, t '..,... ! ' ’ II. The next Great Circle is the Meridian, which is represented by the Brazen Frame or Circle in which the Globe hangs and turns: This is divided into four Nineties, or Degrees, beginning at the BquinoBial, ’ Tis called the Meridian, because when the Sun comes to the South Part of this Cir - cle, ’ tis then Meridies, Mid - Day, or High - Noon, and then the Sun hath its greatest Altitude for that Day, which therefore is called the Meridian Altitude. The Plane of this Circle is perpendicular to the Horizon, and passeth through the South and North Points thereof through the zenith and Nadir, and through the Poles of the World. In it, each way from the EquinoBial on the Celestial Globe, is accounted the North or South Declination of the Sun or Stars; and on the Ter resis i a l, the Latitude of a Place North or South; which is all one Quantity with the Elevation or the Height of the Pole above the Horizon: Because the Distance from the Zenith to the Horizon, being the fame as that between the E - quinoBial and the Poles, if from each you imagine the Distance from the Pole to the Zenith to be taken away, the Latitude must remain equal to the Poles Height. There are two Points of this Circle, each Degrees from the EquinoBial, which are called the Poles of the World; and a Diameter from thence continued through the Center of either Globe, is called the Axis of the Earth or Heavens, on which they are supposed to turn round. These Meridians are various, and change ac - cording to the Longitude of Places; for as soon as ever a Man moves but one Degree, or but a Point to the East or Weft, he is under anew Meridian: But there is ( or should be ) one fix ’ d, which is cal - led the First Meridian. And this on some Globes passes through Gratiofa, one of the Azores Islands; but the French place the First Meridian at Fro, one of the Canary Islands. The Poles of. the Meridian are the East and Weft Points of the Horizon. On the Terrestrial Globe there are usually drawn Twenty four Meridians, one through every De - grees of the Equator, or through every Degrees of Longitude. The Vfes of this Circle are First, To fet the Globe to any particular Latitude,, by a proper Elevation of the Pole above the Horizon of that Place: And, Secondly, To ftiew the Sun or Stars Declination, right Ascension, and greatest Altitude; of which more below. III. The next Great Circle is the EquinoBial, as it is called on the Celestial, and Equator on the Ter - reftrial Globe. This is a great Circle, whose Poles are the Poles of the World: It divides the Globe in - to two equal Parts or Hemispheres, as to North and South; and it passeth through the East and Weft Points of the Horizon, and at the Meridian is al - ways as much raised above the Horizon, as is the Compliment of the Latitude of any particular Place. Whenever the Sun cometh to this Circle, it makes equal Days arid Nights all round the Globe, because it always Rifeth then due East, and Sets due Weft, which it doth at no other Time of the Year. All Stars also which are under this Circle, or which have no Declination, do always Rife due East, and Set full Weft. All People living under this Circle ( which in Ge - grapy, or rather by Navigators, is called the Line ) have the Days and Nights constantly equal; and when the Sun is in the Equinoctial, he will be at Noon in their Zenith, or directly over their Heads,, and so their erect Bodies can east no Shadow. From this Circle, both ways, the Sun or Stars Declination on the Celestial, or Latitude of all Places on the Terrestrial Globe:, is accounted on the Meri - dian: And such lesser Circles as run through each Degree of Latitude or Declination parallel to the Equinoctial, are called Parallels of Latitude, or Parallels of Declination. Through every Degrees of this Equinoctial the Hour - Circles are drawn at Right Angles to it on the Celestial Globe, and all pass through the Poles of the World, dividing the Equinoctial into equal Parts. And the Equator on the Terrestrial Globe is divi - ded by the Meridian into equal Parts; which Meridians are equivalent to the Hour - Circles on the other Globe. IV. The Zgsdiack. is another Great Circle of the Sphere, dividing the Globe into two equal Parts: When the Points of Aries and Libra are brought to the Horizon, it will cut that and the Equinoctial Obliquely, making with the former an Angle equal to the Sun ’ s greatest Meridian Altitude in any Lati - tude; and with the Equinoctial, an Angle equal to Degrees and Minutes, which is the Sim ’ s greatest Declination. This Circle by Astronomers is accounted as a kind of a broad one, and is like a Belt or Girdle round the Globe: Through the Mid - dle of it is drawn a Line called the Ecliptick., or Via Solis, th e Way of the Sun -, because the Sun ne - ver deviates from it in its Annual Motion, as the Planets do all more or less, whence it hath itsBreadth i This Circle is mark ’ d with the Characters of the - Twelve Signs, and on it is found out the Sun ’ s Place, which which is under what Star or Degree of any of the Twelve Zpdaical Cancellations he appears to be at Noon. By this are determined the Four Quarters of the Year, according as the Ecliptick is divided into four equal Parts; and according as the Sun goes on here, he hath more orlefs Declination. Also from this Circle the Latitude of the Planets and fixed Stars are accounted from the Ecliptick to -. wards its Poles. The Poles of this Circle are Degrees Mi - nutes distant from the Poles of the W orld, or of the Equinoctial, and by their Motion round the Poles of the " World, are the Polar Circles described. In these Poles of the Ecliptick all the Circles of Longitude which are drawn through the Zodiack do determinate, as the Meridians and Hour - Circles do in the Poles of the World, and as the Azimuth or Vertical Circles do in the Zenith and Nadir. V. If you imagine two Great Circles palling both through the Poles of the World, and alio one of them through the Equinoctial Points, Aries and Li - bra, and the other through the Soljlitial Points, Can - cer and Capricorn. These are called the two Colures, the one the Equi - noctial, the other the Soljlitial Colure. These will divide the Ecliptick into four equal Parts or Quar - ters, which are denominated according to the Points where these pass through, called the Four Cardinal Points, and are the first Points of Aries, Libra, Can - cer, and Capricorn. These are all the Great Circles. VI. If you suppose two Circles drawn parallel to the Equinoctial, at Degrees Minutes di - stant from it, one towards the North, the other towards the South, these are called the Tropickj, be - cause the Sun appears, when in them, to turn back - ward from his " former Course, the one the Tropick of Cancer, and the other the Tropick of Capricorn, because they are under these Signs. VII. If two other Circles are supposed to be drawn through Degrees Minutes, reckoned on the Meridian from the Polar Points, these are called the Polar Circles: The Northern is the Artick, and the Southern the Antartick Circles, because opposite to the former. These are the Pour Lesser Circles. And these on the T terrestrial G ' be the Ancients supposed to divide the Earth into Five Zpnes, vig. two Frigid, two Temperate, and the Torrid Zpne. Besides these Ten Circles lately described, which are always drawn on the Globe it self, there are some other necessary Circles to be known, which are barely imaginary, and supposed only to be drawn upon the G lobe. j. Meridians, or Hour - Circles, which are great Circles meeting all in the Poles of the World, and crossing the Equinoctial at Right Angles; these are supplied by theMeridian, Hour - Circle, and Index. . Azimuths, or Vertical Circles, which likewise are Great Circles of the Sphere, and meet in the Zp - with and Nadir, as the Meridians and Hour - Circles do in the Poles: These cut the Horizon at Right Angles, and on these is reckoned the Sun ’ s Altitude when he is not in the Meridian. They are rere - sented by the Quadrant of Altitude, which being fix ’ d at the Zenith, is moveable about round the Globe through all the Points of the Compass. .. There are also Circles of Longitude of the Stars and Planets, which are Great Circles passing thro ' f the Pole of the Ecliptick, and in that Line deters mining the Stars or Planets Place or Lon tude reckoned from the first Point of Aries. Almacanters, or Parallels of Altitude are Cir - cles having their Poles in the Zenith, and are al - ways drawn parallel to the Horizon. These are Lesser Circles of the Sphere, diminishing gradually as they go farther and farther from the Horizon. In rested of the Stars there are also supposed to be Parallels of Latitude, which are parallel to the Ecliptick, and have their Poles the fame with those of that Circle. . Parallels of Declination of the Sun or Stars which are lesser Circles, whose Poles are the Poles of the World, and are all drawn parallel to the E - quinodial, either North or South and these ( when drawn on the terrestrial Globe ) are called Parallels of Latitude definitions. . Latitude of any Place, is an Arch of the Me - dian of that Place, intercepted between its Zenith and the Equator and this is the fame with an Arch, of the Meridian, intercepted between the Pole and the Horizon; and therefore it is often expressed by the Poles Height, or Elevation of the Pole: The Realbn of which is, Thatfrom the Equator to the Pole, there always being the Distance of De - grees, and from the Zenith to the Horizon the fame Number, and each of thele Degrees containing within it the Distance between the Zenith and the Pole; that Distance therefore being taken away from both, must leave the Distance from the Zenith to the Equator, equal to the Distance between the Pole and the Horizon, or to the Elevation of the Pole above the Horizon. . Latitude of a Star or Planet, is an Arch of a Great Circle reck ned on the Quadrant of Altitude, laid through the Star and Pole of the Ecliptick, from the Ecliptick towards its Pole. . Longitude of a Place, is an Arch of the Equator intercepted between the Meridian of the Place and the first Meridian: Or it is more properly the Difference, either East or Weft, between the Meridians of any two Places, accounted on the E - quator. . Longitude of a Star, is an Arch of the Ecliptic, accounted from the beginning of Aries to the Place where the Stars Circle of Longitude croffeth the Ecliptick; so that it is much the fame as the Stars place in the Ecliptick, accounted from the be - ginning of Aries. . Amplitude of the Sun, or of a Star, is an Arch of the Horizon intercepted between the true East or Weft Points of it, and that Point upon which the Sun or Star Rises or Sets. . Eight Ascension of the Sun, or of a Star, is that part of the Equinoctial reckoned from the beginning of Aries, which Rifeth or Setteth with the Sun or Star in a Right Sphere: But in an Oblique Sphere it is that Part or Degree of the Equinoctial which comes to the Meridian with it, ( as before ) reckoned from the beginning of Aries. . A Eight or DireB Sphere, is when the Poles are in the Horizon, and the Equator in the Zenith. The Consequence of being under such a Position of the Heavens as this ( which is the Case of those who livediredly under the Line ) is, That the Inhabitants have no Latitude nor Elevation of the Pole: They can nearly fee both the Pole of the World: All the ' Stars G L O G LO Scars in the Heavens do once in Hours Rife, Calumniate, and Set with them; the Sun always Rises and Descends at Right Angles with the Hori - zon, which is the Reason they have always equal Day and Night, because the Horizon doth exactly kissed the Circle of the Sun ’ s Diurnal Revolution. . A Parallel Sphere, is where the Poles are in the Zenith and Nadir, and the Equinoctial in the Hori - zon which is the Case of iuch Persons, if any such ’ there be, who live directly under the North or South Poles. ' And the Consequences of iuch a Portion are, That the Parallels of the Sun ’ s Declination will also be Parallels of his Altitude, or Almacanters to them. The Inhabitants can fee only such Stars as are on their Side the Equinoctial; and they must have months Day, and Months continual Night every ear; and the Sun can never be higher with them than Degrees Minutes ( which is not so high as it is with us on February oth. ) . An Oblique Sphere, is where the Pole is eleve - ted to any Number of Degrees less than: And Consequently the Axis of the Globe can never be at Right Angles to, nor in the Horizon; and the E - quator, and Parallels of Declination, will all cut rite Horizon Obliquely, from whence it takes its Name., o, n Oblique Ascension of the Sun, or Stars, is that I art or Degree of the Equinoctial reckoned from the beginning of Aries, which Rises and Sets with them in ah Oblique Sphere. Afcentional Difference, is the Difference between the Bjght and Oblique Ascension, when the Lesser is subtracted from the Greater. On the Terreftnal Globe. . A Space upon the Surface of the Earth, rec - zoned between two Parallels to the Equator, wherein the Increase of the longest Day is a Quar - ter of an Hour, is by some Writers called a Parallel. . And the Space contained between two such Parallels, is called a Climate These Climates be - gin at the Equator; and when we go thence North or South, till the Day become half an Hour longer than it was before, they fay, we are come into the First Climate; when the Days are an Hour longer than they are under the Equator, we are come to the Second Climate, &c. These Climates are ac - counted in Number, reckoned each way to - wards the Poles. The Inhabitants of the Earth are divided into three forts, as to the falling of their Shadows. . Amphiscii, who are thole which inhabit the Torrid Zpne, or live between the Equator and To - picks, and consequently have the Sun twice a Year in their Zenith; at which time they are Ajcii, i. e. have no Shadows, the Sun being Vertical to them. These have their Shadows call to the Southward, when the Sun is in the Northern Signs; and to the Northward, when the Sun sin the Southern Signs, reckoned in rested of them. . Heteroscii, who are those whole Shadows fall but one way; as is the Case of all such as live be - tween the Tropicks and Polar Circles: For their Sha - dows at Noon are always to the Northward in North Latitude, and to the Southward in South Latitude. . Periscii, are such Persons that inhabit those Places of the Earth that lie between the Polar Cir - cles and the Poles, and therefore have their Sha - dows falling all manner of ways, because the Sun at some times of tnc Year goes clear round about them. The Inhabitants of the Earth, in respect ol one another, are also divided into three forts. . Periled, who are such as inhabiting the fame Parallel ( not a Great Circle ) are yet directly oppo - lite to one another, the one being East or Weft from the other exa & ly Degrees, which is theft Difference of Longitude: Now these have the fame Latitude and Length of Days and Nights, but exactly at contrary Times for when the Sun Rifeth to one, it Sets to the other. . Antced, who are Inhabitants of such Places, as being under a Semi - circle of the fame Meridian do lie at equal Distances from the Equator, one to - wards the North, and the other towards the South. / Now these have the fame Degree of Latitude, but towards contrary Parts, the one North, and the other South - and therefore must have the Seasons of the Year directly at contrary times one to the other. . Antipodes, who are such as dwell under the fame Meridian, but in two opposite and equi - di - stant Parallels, and in the two opposite Points of those two Parallels; so that they go Feet against Feet, and are distant from each other an entire Di - ameter of the Earth, or Degrees of a Great Circle. These have the lame Degree of Latitude, but the one South, the other North, and accounted from the Equator a quite contrary way and there - fore these will have all things, as Day and Night, Summer and Winter, directly contrary to one ano - ther,. PROBLEMS. I. To find the Latitude of any Place. Bring the Place to the Brass Meridian, and the Degrees of that Circle, intercepted between the Place and the Equinoctial, are the Latitude of that Place either North or South. Then to fit the Globe lo that the Wooden Horizon flail represent the Horizon of that Place, elevate the Pole as many Degrees above the Wooden Hori - zon, as are the Latitude of that Place, and it is done; for then will that Place be in the Zenith. If after this you reiffify the Globe to any particular Time, you may by the Index know the Tjtne of Sun - riling and Setting with the Inhabitants of that Place, and consequently the prelect Length of their Day and Night, PROBLEM It To find the Longitude of Places; .. - Bring the Places severally to the Brass Meridian, ’ and then the Number of Degrees of the EquinoSli - al, which are between the Meridians of each Place, are their Difference of Longitude either East or Weft. PROBLEM III. For the Dijlances of Places on the Terrejlrial Globe. See the Problem on the Celestial Globe, For find - ing the Dijiancc between two Stars. PROBLEM IV. To find what Places of the Earth the Sun is Vertical to at any time assigned. Bring the Suns Place, found in the Ecliptick on the Terrestrial Globe, to the Brazen Meridian, and note what Degree of the Meridian it cuts; then by turning the Globe round about, you will fee what Places of the Earth are in that Parallel of De - clination, ( for they will all come fuccelTively to that Degree of the Brazen Meridian ) and thole are the Places or Parts of the Earth to which the Sun will be Vertical that Day; whose Inhabitants w'ill then be Ascii, that is, their eredfc Bodies at Noon will call no Shadow. Problems on the Celestial Globe. Suppose May the both, i oi, the Sun ’ s Place to be Just at the Entrance into the first Degree of Gemini. PROBLEM I. To rubify the Globe: Or, To render it in the General fit to resolve any Problem; which Rectification therefore is always supposed to be the first thing done: To do which, Bring the Sun ’ s Place, found in the Ecliptick on the Globe, to the Meridian, and the Hour - Index to at Noon. PROBLEM II. For the Suns Declination ' Bring the Sun ’ s Place for that Day, ( " which here and below is supposed to be given ) to the Meridi - an as before, and then the Degrees of the Meridian, reckoned from the EquinoRial eitherNorth or South, are the Suns Declination at Noon, either North or South, according to the Time of the Year, vi. from March the loth to September the th, North; and thence to March again South: And the Decli - nation for May the th will be Degrees and a - bout Minutes North. PROBLEM III. For his Amplitude either Fjfmg or Setting. Bring the Sun ’ s Place to the Horizon, either on the East or Weft Side, and the Degrees of the Hori - zon, accounted from the East Point, either North or South, are the Amplitude required, vi. May the th, the Sun ’ s Amplitude will be Degrees to the North of the East. And at the fame time you have in the outer Cir - cle of Rhumbs the Point which the Sun Rises or Sets upon, N. E. by E. or N. W. by W. PROBLEM IV. For his PJght Afcenfm. Bring the Sun ’ s Place to the Meridian, and the Number of Degrees intercepted between the be - ginning of Aries, and that Degree of the Equinoctial, which comes to the Meridian with the Sun, is the Eight Afccnjion. " ' r " " " " ’ If you would have it in Time, account every Degrees to be an Hour, and every Degree to be Minutes. N. B. The Reason of bringing the Sun ’ s Place to the Meridian in this Problem, is to save the Trouble of putting the Globe into the Position of a Eight Sphere: For properly, Right Ascension is that Degree of the Equinoctial which Rises with the Sun in a Bjght Sphere. But since the Equator is always at Right Angles to the Meridian, if you bring the Sun ’ s Place thither, it must in the Equinoctial cut his Right Ascension: Thus in the Instance of May the oth, the Sun ’ s Right Ascension will be De - grees, or Hours wanting Minutes. PROBLEM V. For the Oblique Ascension: Bring the Sun ’ s Place to the Horizon on the East - side, and the Number of Degrees intercepted be - tween that Degree of the Equinoctial which is now come to the Horizon, and the beginning or first Point of Aries is the Oblique Ascension. Thus, May the th, the Sun ’ s Oblique Ascension is Degrees Minutes; Of those two Ascensions take the Lesser from the Greater, the Remainder will be, PROBLEM VI. The Ascensional Difference. Which therefore is the Difference in Degrees be - tween the Right or Oblique Ascension, or the Space between the Sun ’ s Riling and Setting, and the Hour of Six: Wherefore his Ascensional Difference turn - ed into Time, will give the Time of the Sun ’ s Ri - ling or Setting before or after Six. Thus, from Degrees take Degrees Minutes, there will remain Degrees Minutes, the Ascensional Dis - ference in Degrees, and in Time Hour Minutes; and so much doth the Sun Rife before Six, and Set after it. PROBLEM VII. For the Suns Effing or Setting. Bring his Place to the Horizon, either East or Weft, and the Hour - Index shall shew the Time ei - ther of his Riling or Setting accordingly; which. May the oth, is Minutes after in the Morning, and Minutes before at Night. The Time of the Sun ’ s Setting doubled, gives the Length of the Day, which the with be Hours Minutes; and the Time of this Riling doubled, gives the Length of the Night, which. May the oth, is Hours Minutes. PROBLEM VIII. For the Suns Meridian Altitude, or Deprejfion at Midnight. Bring his place to the Meridian, above the Hori - zon, for his Noon Altitude, which will shew the Degrees of it accounted there from the Horizon; which, May the th, will be Degrees Mi - nutes. For his Midnight Depression, below the North Point of the Horizon, you must bring the Point in the Ecliptick, opposite to the Sun ’ s present place, to the South part of the Meridian above the Horizon; and the Degrees there intercepted be - tween that Point and the Horizon, are his Midnight DeprelEon G, LO Depredion which, May the oth, will be De - grees Minutes. PROBLEM IX. For the Stlris Altitude at any Time of the Day given. FeBify the Globe, and fit the Quadrant of Altitude that is, screw the Brass Quadrant of Altitude to the Zenith; or in our Latitude, screw it so that the graduated Edge cut Degrees Minutes on the Meridian, reckoned from the Equinoctial. Then turn about the Globe till the Index shew the Time proposed, and stay the Globe there; af - ter which bring the Quadrant of Altitude to cut the Sun ’ s Place in the Ecliptick, and then that Place or Degree of the Ecliptick shall shew the Sim ’ s Al - titude on the Quadrant. Thus, May the oth, the Sun ’ s Altitude at Nine a Clock in the Morning will be Degrees Minutes. PROBLEM X. To find the SunsHour or Altitude when he is due Eajl or Well above the Horizon. FeBify the Globe, and fit the Quadrant of Alti - tude j then bring the Quadrant to cut the true Eaji Point, and next turn the Globe about till the Sun ’ s Place in the Ecliptick cut the graduated Edge of the Quadrant, for then that Place will shew the Al - titude and the Index of the Hour. Thus, May the i oth, the Sun will be East at Minutes past Seven in the Morning, and his Alti - tude then is Degrees: PROBLEMS To find the Suns Altitude or Time of the Day on any Azimuth given Or, When the Sun is on any given Point of the Compass. Set the Quadrant of Altitude to the Azimuth gi - ven, then turn the Globe till his place in the Ecliptic touch the graduated Edge of the Quadrant; so shall that place give the Altitude on the Quadrant, and the Hour - Index the Time of the Day. Example. May the th, the Azimuth being Degrees from the South toward the East, or the Point of the Compass which the Sun is then on being S. E. by E. and near half a Point more Easterly; his Alti - tude will be ( nearly ) Degrees, and the Hour of the Day a little more than a Quarter past Nine in the Morning. PROBLEM XII. To find the Declination and Fight Ascension of any Star. Bring the Star to the Meridian, and then the De - grees intercepted between the Equinoctial and the Point of the Meridian cut by the Star, are its De - clination; and the Meridian cuts and shews its Might Ascension on the EquinoBial, accounting it from the beginning of Aries PROBLEM XIII. To find the Longitude and Latitude of any Star l Bring the Solstitial Colure to the Brass Meridian and there fix the Globe; then will the Pole of the Ecliptick be just under Degrees Minutes, ac - counted from the Pole above the North Point of the Horizon, and upon the fame Meridian; there screw the Quadrant of Altitude, and then bring its grade - ated Edge to the Star Jaftigned, and there stay it so will the Star cut its proper Latitude on the Qua - drant, reckoned from the Ecliptick s and the Qua - drant will cut the Ecliptick in the Star ’ s Longitude or its Distance from the first Point of Aries PROBLEM XIV. To find the Time of any Stars Fifing, Setting, or Cul - minating, i. e. being on the Meridian. FpBify the Globe and Hour - Index, and bring the Star to the East or Weft part of the Horizon, or to the Brazen Meridian, and the Index will shew ac - cordingly the Time of the Star ’ s Pjfing, Setting, or Culminating, or of its being on the Meridian. Thus, May the oth, ArBurus will be on the Me - ! ridian at about i of an Hour after o at Night; Cor Leonis will be Setting about one in the Morning; and the first Star in the Head of Aries will be Effing about an Hour after. PROBLEM XV. To know, at any Time assigned, what Stars are Fifing or Setting; what are on the Meridian, and how high they are above the Horizon; and on what Ai - much or Point of the Compass they are j by which means the real Stars in the Heaven may easily be known by their proper Names, and rightly difiin - guifhed one from another FeBify the Globe, and fit the Quadrant of Altitude and fet the Globe, by the Means of the Compass, due North and South j then turn the Globe ancj. Hour - Index to the Hour of the Night assigned j so will the Globe, thus fix ’ d, represent the Face or Ap - pearance of the Heavens for that Time. Whereby you may readily fee what Stars are in Or near the Horizon; what are on or near the Meri - dian; which are to the North or which to the South, &c. And the Quadrant of Altitude being laid over any particular Star, will shew its Altitude and Azimuth, and on what Point of the Compass it is; whereby any Star may easily be known, efpeci - ally if you have a Quadrant, or any such Instrument, to take the Altitude of any real Star supposed to be known by the Globe, to fee whether it agree with that Star which is its Representative on the Globe or not. PROBLEM XVI. Given the Suns Place, and any Stars Altitude, to find the Hour of the Night, FeBify the Globe and fit the Quadrant, then move the Globe to and fro till the Quadrant cut the Star in its given Altitude, for then the Hour - Index will shew the Hour of the Night: And thus may X k. the Ate the Hour of the Night, be known by a Star ’ s Ai - much. or its Azimuth from its Altitude. Example. May the i cth, the Sun being in the first Degree of Gemini, I take the Altitude of Lucida Lyra, which I find to be Degrees, or I find its Azimuth to be two Degrees to the Northward of the East; then bringing the Quadrant of Altitude to cut that Star in Degrees of Altitude, I find the Hour - Index points at Eleven a Clock at Night; as it would also have done had the Star been brought to the Ai - much on the Globe. PROBEM XVII. To find the Distance between any two Stars. If the Stars lie both under the fame Meridian, bring them to the Brazen Meridian, and the De - grees between them there reckoned are their true Pittance, Thus Capella, or the Star in the Left Shoulder of Auriga, and Ejgel, which is in Orion's Left Thigh, are nearly unto the fame Meridian; and being both brought to the Brazen Meridian of the Globe, their Pittance there will be found to be Degrees. If they are both in the Equinoctial, or have both the fame Declination, i. e. are both in the fame Parallel, then bring them one alter another to the Brazen Meridian, and the Degrees of the Equinoctial intercepted between them, when thus brought to the Meridian severally, are their Pittance. If the Stars are neither under the lame Meridian, nor parallel, then either lay the Quadrant of Alti - tude from one to the other, ( if it will reach ) and that will shew the Distance between them in De - grees; or else take the Distance with Compasses, and apply that to the Equinoctial, or to the Meri - dian. Which Method of Proceeding also will shew the Pittance of any two Places on the Terrestrial Globe in Degrees; and by Multiplication by, you will have it in Miles. Wherefore to find how far any place on the Globe is from another, you need only take the Distance between them on the Globe with a pair of Compasses; and applying theCompaffes to the Equator at the beginning of Aries, or at the first Meridian, you will there find the Degrees; which multiply by, and that will turn it into Miles. Thus the Distance between London and Jamaica being on the Globe Degrees, I multiply that by, and it gives me Miles; and so far is Ja - manica distant directly from London, or in an Arch of a Great Circle.
